source_metadata.title: Description and Evaluation of the Implementation of a Weight-Based, Nurse-Driven Heparin Nomogram in a Tertiary Academic Medical Center
source_metadata.source_type: Original Article; retrospective pre/post implementation evaluation

atoms.canonical_statement: The article describes institution-wide implementation of a weight-based, nurse-driven UFH management approach during transition to a new EHR and evaluates whether standardization, faster therapeutic anticoagulation, and patient-safety goals were met.

The practice change was implemented institution-wide at Brigham and Women’s Hospital, a 793-bed tertiary academic medical center, for adult patients receiving therapeutic continuous-infusion UFH when a protocol aPTT target was considered appropriate.

population.label: Adult therapeutic-UFH patients at Brigham and Women’s Hospital

atoms.canonical_statement: BWH adopted two noncustomizable, institution-wide, nurse-driven, weight-based UFH nomograms targeting different aPTT ranges.

concept.text: Institution-wide nurse-driven weight-based continuous-infusion unfractionated heparin nomogram

exposures.details: Partners eCare/BWH nomogram with protocolized aPTT monitoring and nurse titration

atoms.canonical_statement: For acute PE or DVT, the nomogram targeted an aPTT range of 60 to 80 seconds.

concept.text: BWH 60-80 second UFH nomogram

exposures.details: Approved for acute PE or DVT; target aPTT 60-80 seconds

atoms.canonical_statement: For acute ACS, the nomogram targeted an aPTT range of 50 to 70 seconds.

concept.text: BWH 50-70 second UFH nomogram

exposures.details: Approved for acute ACS; target aPTT 50-70 seconds

atoms.canonical_statement: Protocol aPTT monitoring was scheduled 6 hours after any heparin dose adjustment and every 6 hours until two consecutive therapeutic aPTTs, after which monitoring was extended to every 12 hours.
Clinicians could use an initial UFH bolus of 80 units/kg with the 60-80 second nomogram or 60 units/kg with the 50-70 second nomogram.

concept.text: Initial UFH bolus for 60-80 second nomogram

exposures.details: Optional initial bolus

concept.text: Initial UFH bolus for 50-70 second nomogram

exposures.details: Optional initial bolus

atoms.canonical_statement: Bolus doses embedded in the titration nomogram for subtherapeutic aPTT values were noncustomizable and could not be removed from the order set.
Unit-based clinical pharmacists and nurse educators monitored UFH daily using the EHR, daily reports, and a computerized clinical surveillance system.
Nomogram implementation coincided with deployment of a new EHR and was preceded by approximately 6 months of multidisciplinary education focused heavily on nursing.
Implementation interventions included a mandatory nursing learning module, updated smart infusion pump libraries, and unit-based nursing education.

On implementation day, nurse-pharmacist teams used safety checklists to verify patient conversion, and postimplementation records were reviewed daily to assess correct nomogram use and provide one-on-one education.

The evaluation used a retrospective pre-versus-post design comparing internal quality-assurance data from September-November 2013 and 2014 with nomogram-treated patients from September 2015 after a 3-month wash-in period.
The primary endpoint was elapsed time to minimum-threshold therapeutic anticoagulation, defined as reaching the lower limit of the selected aPTT goal range (50 or 60 seconds).

concept.text: Time to minimum-threshold therapeutic anticoagulation

outcome.definition: Elapsed time to reach the lower limit of the selected aPTT therapeutic goal range (50 or 60 seconds)

atoms.canonical_statement: A secondary endpoint was the proportion of patients reaching therapeutic anticoagulation within 24 hours of UFH.

concept.text: Therapeutic anticoagulation within 24 hours

atoms.canonical_statement: A safety endpoint was the proportion of patients with a critically supratherapeutic aPTT of at least 120 seconds while receiving UFH.

concept.text: Critically supratherapeutic aPTT

atoms.canonical_statement: In the postnomogram period, patients were excluded when nonnomogram provider-driven UFH titration was used.
In the prenomogram period, patients were excluded when UFH was used without a specified aPTT goal.

population.label: Prenomogram-period UFH patients

atoms.canonical_statement: The study reported 93% power to detect a 30% change in the primary endpoint at alpha 0.05.

Time-to-event analysis used the log-rank test with Kaplan-Meier estimation; categorical data used chi-square tests, continuous parametric data used Student t tests, and the first four postnomogram aPTTs were summarized descriptively.
Figure 1 reports 1,256 patients evaluated, 412 included, and 844 excluded; included patients comprised 317 prenomogram and 95 postnomogram patients.
The Results text reports 1,255 patient records evaluated, 844 excluded, and 411 included, while also listing 317 prenomogram and 95 postnomogram patients.

atoms.canonical_statement: The authors identify the retrospective design as a study limitation.
Potential documentation inaccuracies and undocumented bedside changes limited the ability to account for provider-driven noncompliance with the nomogram.
Unequal prenomogram and postnomogram group sizes were considered a potential confounding factor.
The pre-versus-post design lacked a concurrent true comparator and was susceptible to chronological bias and baseline patient differences.
The study did not differentiate critically ill from noncritically ill patients, which the authors note could confound the data.
Institution-wide standardization was incomplete because numerous services continued to use provider-driven custom UFH infusions.
The authors conclude that the weight-based, nurse-driven UFH nomogram produced faster therapeutic anticoagulation without increasing critically high aPTT values.

The authors state that institution-wide UFH nomograms can be implemented alongside a new EHR when a dedicated multidisciplinary team, substantial education, and close implementation monitoring are present.
Jean Connors reported consulting for Bristol Meyer Squibb and serving on Scientific Advisory Boards for Bristol Meyer Squibb and Boehringer Ingelheim.
The authors reported receiving no financial support for the research, authorship, or publication of the article.
Supplementary material was stated to be available online, but it was not contained in the retrieved raw PDF.
